title: Apple Ordered to Stop Using Scare Screens Against Third-Party Payment Apps
excerpt: A U.S. judge found Apple violated a court injunction by using alarming warnings and barriers to push users away from cheaper payment alternatives outside the App Store.
body:
• A U.S. federal judge ruled Apple violated a 2021 court injunction by using "scare screens" and other barriers to discourage users from third-party payment systems.
  • Apple must immediately stop charging commissions on off-app purchases and remove all restrictions on how developers link to external payment options.
  • The ruling stems from the Epic Games v. Apple case and could reshape how iPhone and iPad users pay for apps and subscriptions in the United States.
  • Fortnite will return to the U.S. App Store following the decision, with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney calling it "a significant win for developers and consumers."

Judge Finds Apple in Contempt of 2021 Order

U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple deliberately violated a 2021 injunction designed to allow app developers to direct users to third-party payment options outside the App Store. The judge found that Apple, rather than complying with the order, "imposed new barriers and new requirements to increase friction and increase breakage rates with full page 'scare' screens, static URLs, and generic statements."

https://x.com/snrckrd/status/2089414778712179017

The original injunction, issued as part of the landmark Epic Games v. Apple antitrust case, prohibited Apple from blocking developers' ability to communicate with and direct consumers to alternative purchasing mechanisms. The court found that Apple's 30% commission "allowed it to reap supracompetitive operating margins" not tied to its own intellectual property.

"Apple's continued attempts to interfere with competition will not be tolerated. This is an injunction, not a negotiation. There are no do-overs once a party wilfully disregards a court order."

— Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, U.S. District Court

What Apple Must Change

The ruling imposes sweeping requirements on Apple's App Store practices in the United States. The company is now barred from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app, and cannot require developers to report such external transactions.

Apple can no longer restrict the style, language, formatting, or placement of links to external payment options. Developers are free to use buttons and calls to action directing users to cheaper alternatives. The company must also allow dynamic links that take consumers directly to product pages in a logged-in state, rather than forcing generic landing pages.

The most pointed requirement addresses Apple's controversial warning screens. The judge ordered that Apple may only display "a neutral message apprising users that they are going to a third-party site," effectively banning the alarming red-exclamation-mark alerts that critics called scare tactics designed to frighten users away from non-Apple payment processors.

A Pattern of Resistance

Apple's use of aggressive warning screens had drawn widespread criticism from developers and regulators. When the EU's Digital Markets Act required Apple to allow alternative payment systems in Europe, the company displayed a critical-level alert — the most severe type in its own design guidelines, normally reserved for situations like potential data loss — on apps using third-party payment processors such as Stripe or PayPal.

According to a report from 9to5Mac, Apple had proposed a toned-down disclosure sheet in August 2024, replacing the red exclamation icon with a gray information icon. Apple told the outlet it was ready to implement the changes, but the EU requested the company hold off and never followed up. The EU subsequently fined Apple $500 million for noncompliance.

In a separate development, Apple also recently lost its challenge against the EU's designation of its App Stores and iOS as "gatekeeper" platforms under the DMA. The Luxembourg-based General Court dismissed all of Apple's actions, confirming Apple must continue allowing rival services to interoperate with its platforms.

What Comes Next

Apple has said it will appeal the decision but will comply with the ruling in the meantime. "We strongly disagree with the decision. We will comply with the court's order and we will appeal," the company told MacRumors.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called the ruling "a significant win for developers and consumers," noting that it "forces Apple to compete with other payment services rather than blocking them." Sweeney confirmed Fortnite will return to the U.S. App Store and offered to drop all current and future litigation if Apple extends the framework worldwide.

For consumers, the practical impact could be significant. Without Apple's 30% commission on external purchases, apps like Netflix, Spotify, and gaming platforms could offer lower subscription prices through direct payment links. Services that previously removed App Store payment options entirely — forcing users to navigate to websites on their own — can now link directly to their payment pages from within the app.
nri_angle: The ruling could lower app subscription costs for millions of iPhone users worldwide, including diaspora communities who rely heavily on mobile payment platforms.
